contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Two indices are only a representation. Classification requires the maintained candidate and invariant; the same names can implement two pointers, sliding window, a range query, or neither.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: What is the strongest review of the claim “the solution uses two indices, so it is a two-pointers problem”?

options.text: Reject it: two indices are a representation, and classification requires the candidate and movement invariant.
Accept it: two indices are the definition of two pointers.
Accept it whenever the loop is O(n).
Accept it when the variables are named left and right.

feedback.reason: The number and names of indices do not specify what the algorithm maintains or why movement is safe.

blocks.text: Two indices can bound a sliding window, delimit a binary-search interval, identify a range query, coordinate a merge, or serve read/write roles. These algorithms differ because their candidates, state, and discard proofs differ. Calling all of them two pointers removes the diagnostic information Patternly is meant to teach. The correct process is to ask what the indices mean, which elements belong to the current candidate, and what theorem justifies each movement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_definition: This definition collapses windows, binary-search intervals, merges, and read/write scans into one category, erasing the distinct invariants that justify movement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_if_linear: Many linear algorithms are not two pointers, and complexity does not determine family.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_names: Identifier names are arbitrary implementation details; they do not establish candidate membership, maintained state, or a safe discard rule.

constraints: Treat “two pointers” as a diagnostic family label, not as a literal count of index variables.

items.prompt: Code maintains a frequency map for s[left..right], expands right, and advances left while a character count exceeds a limit. A learner labels it two pointers because two indices move. What correction is required?

options.text: It is sliding window because the map and validity rule belong to the entire contiguous range.
The learner is correct because exactly two indices move.
The labels are interchangeable in all technical discussions.
A frequency map means neither family applies.

feedback.reason: Explicit range-owned state and validity repair outweigh the superficial two-index cue.

blocks.text: left and right identify the members of one current substring, while the frequency map records state for all of them. When the predicate fails, removing left characters repairs that same candidate. Those are window semantics. The phrase “two pointers” is sometimes used informally for any two-boundary loop, but this learning taxonomy reserves it for endpoint, convergence, or read/write relations so that the distinction remains diagnostically useful.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers_count: Counting indices ignores that both boundaries delimit one substring whose full frequency state is maintained and repaired after violations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_same: The product intentionally distinguishes the families because their proofs and transfer boundaries differ.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.neither_map: Auxiliary state does not exclude a family; here it is precisely the window state.

constraints: The frequency map exactly matches the current substring.

items.prompt: Select all examples that contain two indices but should not be classified as the two-pointers family under the stated invariant.

options.text: left and right bound a contiguous range with a maintained sum and a shrink-to-valid rule.
l and r are supplied once to compute prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l].
left and right form a sorted endpoint pair, and a comparison safely eliminates one endpoint.
read scans input while write marks the next compacted output position.

feedback.reason: One example is a sliding window and the other is a direct range query; both refute the index-count heuristic.

blocks.text: The window example uses two boundaries but belongs to sliding window because the full range is maintained and repaired. The prefix-query example also uses two indices, yet they are immutable query parameters rather than moving pointers or a window. By contrast, the sorted pair example has an endpoint-elimination invariant and the read/write example has a same-direction two-pointers invariant. The presence of a valid counterexample outside both families is important: the correct classifier must permit “neither.”

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_pair_example: This example does have a two-pointers invariant because sorted comparison justifies endpoint elimination.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_write_example: Distinct read and write roles form a canonical same-direction two-pointers invariant.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sliding_window_example: Omitting this preserves the false claim that every two-boundary moving loop is two pointers.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_query_example: Omitting this misses that two indices may describe a range without either moving-pointer family.

constraints: More than one statement may be correct.

items.prompt: A prompt says only that an O(n) solution uses indices i and j, with no output contract, state description, or movement rule. What classification is warranted?

options.text: Neither family can be assigned yet; inspect the candidate, maintained state, and movement proof.
Two pointers, because i and j are two indices.
Sliding window, because two indices can bound a range.
Ask only whether the indices move toward each other.

feedback.reason: Without candidate semantics or a discard proof, any family label would be a guess.

blocks.text: Complexity and variable count are compatible with many algorithms. To classify two pointers, the prompt must reveal an endpoint, convergence, merge, or read/write relation and explain safe movement. To classify sliding window, it must reveal a contiguous candidate, state representing that candidate, and a valid expand/evict or shrink rule. Direction may provide a weak clue but cannot replace these facts. The disciplined response is to request or derive the missing contract before choosing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers: The indices may serve unrelated roles, including a query range or binary-search interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sliding_window: Bounding a geometric range does not prove that the range is the maintained candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.choose_by_direction: Pointer direction has counterexamples in both families and cannot supply the missing invariant.

constraints: Do not infer unstated properties from conventional variable names.

items.prompt: A binary-search implementation keeps low and high indices and discards half the remaining sorted range after each comparison. Why should it not be classified as the two-pointers family merely because two indices move?

options.text: The indices delimit a search interval and the invariant discards value ranges by a midpoint test; they do not represent a pair whose relation is being optimized.
It is two pointers because any two changing indices define that family.
It is two pointers because binary search is always linear after the first comparison.
It is sliding window because low and high are contiguous indices.

feedback.reason: The same representation can support a different invariant and candidate semantics.

blocks.text: Binary search maintains a candidate value range and uses a monotonic predicate to discard one half. It does not compare two endpoints as a pair, maintain a contiguous data window, or use a read/write relation. Variable count and movement direction are therefore insufficient for family classification. The transfer rule is to identify what is being discarded and why; the invariant, not the names low and high, determines the pattern.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices_definition: Two variables can delimit a search interval, a window, a merge, or unrelated positions; the family requires a movement invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_required: Binary search is logarithmic under its sorted/monotonic precondition, and complexity does not define two pointers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_by_default: A contiguous index range is not automatically a maintained sliding-window candidate.

constraints: Classify by the maintained invariant, not by variable names.

items.prompt: Which evidence distinguishes a genuine sliding-window solution from a generic two-index scan?

options.text: The indices delimit one contiguous candidate, state summarizes that candidate, and expansion or shrinkage preserves a window-validity invariant.
The code declares exactly two integer variables named left and right.
The code runs in O(n), regardless of what the indices represent.
The input contains a contiguous slice somewhere, even if the algorithm never maintains it as a candidate.

feedback.reason: Sliding window is defined by range-owned state and a validity-preserving boundary update, not by the existence of two integers.

blocks.text: The diagnostic question is whether the current candidate is the entire contiguous range between the boundaries. If so, the algorithm must maintain state for that range and update it when right expands or left evicts elements. A pair-search or binary-search loop may also use two indices without these operations. The transfer rule is to inspect the candidate identity and the repair rule together.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_names: Names are arbitrary and do not reveal candidate membership or validity state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_runtime: Many linear scans are not sliding windows, while some window algorithms include other costs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_contiguous_slice: A slice in the input is not a maintained candidate unless the algorithm owns and updates its range state.

constraints: Use candidate membership and invariant as the classification test.

items.prompt: A compaction routine scans with read and write indices, copies an accepted element to nums[write], and advances write only after a keep decision. Which classification is most precise?

options.text: A same-direction two-pointers pattern: read explores input while write marks the next position in the retained prefix.
Sliding window, because the write index is a left boundary of a contiguous candidate.
Binary search, because two indices identify a range of valid output positions.
No pattern applies because the indices do not move toward each other.

feedback.reason: The indices have distinct read/write roles and maintain a compacted-prefix invariant.

blocks.text: read visits every input position, while write identifies where the next retained value belongs. The invariant is that the prefix before write already equals the filtered output. Neither index bounds a range whose aggregate state is repaired, and there is no midpoint elimination. Movement direction is not the defining criterion; the role relation and overwrite safety are.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sliding_window: The routine does not maintain statistics for a current contiguous range; it builds a retained prefix through read/write roles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search: No sorted monotonic predicate or half-range elimination is present.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.not_a_pattern: Same-direction two pointers includes read/write compaction even though the indices never converge.

constraints: The write position advances only when the current value is retained.

items.prompt: A range-sum query receives immutable l and r and returns prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]. Why is this not a moving two-pointers or sliding-window algorithm?

options.text: l and r describe query endpoints but do not move through candidates or maintain an evolving range invariant.
It is sliding window because prefix sums represent a contiguous interval.
It is two pointers because the formula subtracts one index from another.
It is binary search because the endpoints are ordered numerically.

feedback.reason: A range described by two parameters is not automatically a dynamically maintained candidate.

blocks.text: The query endpoints are supplied once and the prefix array answers the range in constant time. There is no endpoint movement, pair comparison, expansion, shrinkage, or eviction invariant. The contiguous mathematical range belongs to the query contract, not to a sliding-window process. The transfer rule is to distinguish a static interval description from an algorithm that evolves its candidate boundaries.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_is_window: Prefix preprocessing can answer ranges without maintaining a live window or repairing a validity predicate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers_by_subtraction: Arithmetic involving two indices is not the same as a two-pointers movement invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search_range: Ordered endpoints alone do not imply midpoint elimination or a monotonic search predicate.

constraints: The query endpoints are fixed for this operation.

items.prompt: Select all statements that correctly reject the heuristic “two indices means two pointers.”

options.text: A binary-search range uses two bounds but classifies by monotonic half elimination.
A fixed range query can use l and r without any moving-pointer invariant.
A window is always two pointers because all ranges with two endpoints belong to the same family.
A read/write compaction scan is a two-pointers pattern despite moving in the same direction.

feedback.reason: The classifier must separate representation from invariant and allow both “two pointers” and “neither” outcomes.

blocks.text: Binary search and fixed range queries demonstrate that two bounds can serve neither moving-pointer family. Read/write compaction demonstrates that a genuine two-pointers pattern need not converge or bound a window. A sliding window is distinct because its range-owned state and validity repair give it a different proof. The reliable test is what each index means, what candidate is maintained, and which movement is safe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_is_same: The statement repeats the heuristic instead of identifying the window-specific state and invariant.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search_counterexample: It shows that two bounds can support a different logarithmic discard invariant.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.static_query_counterexample: It shows that two indices may be fixed parameters rather than moving pointers.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.read_write_is_two_pointers: It prevents the false requirement that two pointers must move toward each other.

constraints: More than one statement is correct.

items.prompt: A reviewer sees an O(n) loop with two integer indices and no explanation of what is discarded. What is the safest next action?

options.text: Request the candidate definition, maintained state, and movement invariant before assigning a family label.
Label it two pointers because the complexity and index count match the common template.
Label it sliding window because every pair of indices spans a range.
Use the variable names to infer whether the method is two pointers or a window.

feedback.reason: Without a candidate and proof of safe movement, a family label is speculation.

blocks.text: O(n) describes a cost bound, not a pattern family. Two indices can support a window, pair search, compaction, binary search, merge, or a static query. The reviewer should ask what the indices represent, which elements remain candidates after a move, and what invariant makes that discard safe. This diagnostic request is more precise than choosing a label from syntax.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.label_two_pointers: Index count and linearity do not establish a two-pointers relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.label_window: Two endpoints do not establish that a live contiguous range and its state are maintained.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.label_by_variable_names: Names are implementation details and can be misleading or absent.

constraints: Do not infer an algorithmic invariant from syntax alone.

items.prompt: Which other algorithm can use two integer indices without being either pair-search two pointers or a sliding window?
constraints: The contrasted algorithm family is defined by state semantics.

options.text: In-place read/write compaction can use read and write indices while maintaining a retained prefix.
Two indices always mean pair search.
Any left/right-like variables define a window.
Two indices always mean binary search.

feedback.reason: The accepted option uses the contrasted invariant rather than surface syntax.

blocks.text: Two variables, linear complexity, and endpoint names appear in both families. Classification depends on whether the candidate is an endpoint relation or a range-owned state and on which movement proof is valid.

items.prompt: What question should a reviewer ask about a pointer move before naming the pattern?
constraints: The contrasted algorithm family is defined by state semantics.

options.text: Which candidates become impossible or which range state is repaired after the move, and why is that safe?
What are the variable names?
How fast is the loop?
Was input sorted?

feedback.reason: The accepted option uses the contrasted invariant rather than surface syntax.

blocks.text: Two variables, linear complexity, and endpoint names appear in both families. Classification depends on whether the candidate is an endpoint relation or a range-owned state and on which movement proof is valid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.name: Names can be misleading.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort: Sortedness is only one possible precondition.

items.prompt: Why is O(n) complexity not enough to classify two-pointer versus sliding-window code?
constraints: The contrasted algorithm family is defined by state semantics.

options.text: Both can be linear, but one may eliminate endpoint candidates while the other maintains aggregate state for a contiguous range.
Linear time proves two pointers.
Linear time proves a window.
Sorting determines the family.

feedback.reason: The accepted option uses the contrasted invariant rather than surface syntax.

blocks.text: Two variables, linear complexity, and endpoint names appear in both families. Classification depends on whether the candidate is an endpoint relation or a range-owned state and on which movement proof is valid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_proves: It proves only a cost bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_window: It proves only a cost bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort: Several families sort or do not sort.

items.prompt: What evidence is sufficient to assign a sliding-window label?
constraints: The contrasted algorithm family is defined by state semantics.

options.text: The candidate is a contiguous interval, state represents its contents, and boundary updates preserve or restore a validity/score invariant.
Two endpoint variables are enough.
A while-loop is enough.
The prompt says interval.

feedback.reason: The accepted option uses the contrasted invariant rather than surface syntax.

blocks.text: Two variables, linear complexity, and endpoint names appear in both families. Classification depends on whether the candidate is an endpoint relation or a range-owned state and on which movement proof is valid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.while: Loop form is not the invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_word: Words do not define implementation state.
